name: Aorta
func: The body's largest artery. It carries oxygen-rich blood from the left ventricle and, through its many branches, delivers it to the head, arms, organs and legs. Its stretchy wall also smooths out each heartbeat's pulse.

levels.kid:
The **aorta** is the biggest blood tube in your whole body, about as wide as a garden hose. It starts at the left side of your heart.

Every time your heart squeezes, it pushes fresh, oxygen-filled blood into the aorta. The aorta goes up a little, bends over like the top of a candy cane, then runs all the way down through your chest and tummy, right in front of your backbone.

Along the way, smaller tubes branch off it, like branches off a tree trunk, carrying blood to your brain, arms, tummy and legs. Its walls are stretchy, like a balloon, so they bounce back after each heartbeat.
levels.hs:
The **aorta** leaves the **left ventricle** through the aortic valve and has four parts.

The **ascending aorta** rises about 5 cm behind the sternum, giving off only the two **coronary arteries**.

The **aortic arch** curves backward and to the left over the **left main bronchus** and the **right pulmonary artery**. Three big branches leave its top: the **brachiocephalic trunk** (which splits into the right subclavian and right common carotid), the **left common carotid** and the **left subclavian** arteries.

The **descending thoracic aorta** runs down the back of the chest on the left side of the vertebral column, next to the esophagus, giving small branches to the ribs, spinal cord, esophagus and bronchi.

It passes through the diaphragm at about the level of the **T12** vertebra (the **aortic hiatus**) and becomes the **abdominal aorta**, which supplies the gut, kidneys and adrenal glands. At about **L4**, near the belly button, it splits into the **left and right common iliac arteries** that head to the pelvis and legs.

Its thick, elastic wall stretches with each beat and recoils afterward, keeping blood moving even between heartbeats.
levels.college:
Key abdominal branches, top to bottom: the **celiac trunk** (about T12; to the stomach, liver, spleen and pancreas), the **superior mesenteric artery** (L1; small intestine to mid-colon), paired **renal arteries** (L1–L2), and the **inferior mesenteric artery** (L3; distal colon and rectum). Paired **lumbar arteries** and the small **median sacral artery** complete the set.

Important relations: the **left renal vein** crosses in front of the aorta just below the SMA, and can be squeezed between them (**nutcracker phenomenon**). The **third part of the duodenum** also lies in that angle. The **inferior vena cava** runs to the right of the abdominal aorta. The **thoracic duct** and **azygos vein** accompany it through the aortic hiatus, which is technically behind the diaphragm, between the crura, so the aorta isn't squeezed when the diaphragm contracts.

The **ligamentum arteriosum**, a remnant of the fetal ductus arteriosus, tethers the arch to the left pulmonary artery. The **left recurrent laryngeal nerve** hooks under the arch beside it, so an arch aneurysm can cause **hoarseness**.

The aortic wall has three layers: **intima**, a thick **media** of elastic lamellae and smooth muscle, and **adventitia** with its own tiny vessels (vasa vasorum). This elasticity is the **Windkessel effect**: storing energy in systole and releasing it in diastole, converting pulsatile ejection into steadier flow.
levels.phd:
The aortic media is built from **lamellar units**: concentric elastic lamellae alternating with smooth muscle cells, linked by fibrillin microfibrils and collagen. The number of lamellar units scales with aortic radius across mammals, keeping tension per unit roughly constant. Elastin is laid down mostly before adulthood and turns over extremely slowly; with age it **fragments and calcifies**, stiffening the aorta. Increased **pulse wave velocity** (a measure of stiffness) brings reflected waves back earlier, raising systolic pressure and cardiac workload, and independently predicts cardiovascular events and even cognitive decline.

**Thoracic aortic aneurysm** genetics center on the smooth muscle **contractile apparatus** and **TGF-β signaling**: **FBN1** (Marfan syndrome), **TGFBR1/2** and **SMAD3** (Loeys–Dietz syndrome), **ACTA2** and **MYH11**. Paradoxically, loss-of-function in TGF-β receptors leads to increased TGF-β signaling in the tissue. Pathology shows **medial degeneration**: elastic fiber loss, smooth muscle dropout and proteoglycan pools.

**Abdominal aortic aneurysm** is different: an inflammatory, degenerative disease driven by smoking, age and atherosclerosis, with macrophage **MMP-9** and **MMP-2** digesting elastin and collagen, and adventitial lymphocytes. Smoking is the strongest modifiable risk factor; diabetes, oddly, is protective.

The arch develops from the embryonic **pharyngeal arch arteries**: the left fourth arch artery forms the arch; abnormal regression produces variants such as a **right-sided arch**, a **double arch**, or an **aberrant right subclavian artery** that passes behind the esophagus.
levels.expert:
**Aortic dissection** presents with sudden **tearing chest pain radiating to the back**, a **difference in blood pressure between the arms**, pulse deficits and sometimes stroke or limb ischemia. A tear in the intima lets blood split the media into a false lumen. The **Stanford classification**: **Type A** involves the ascending aorta and is a surgical emergency (risk of rupture into the pericardium, coronary occlusion, aortic regurgitation); **Type B** starts beyond the left subclavian and is often managed medically unless complicated. Dissection can extend into the carotids (stroke) or compromise **spinal cord** arteries (paraplegia). **CT angiography** is the key test; a widened mediastinum on chest X-ray is a clue.

**Abdominal aortic aneurysm** may be felt as a **pulsatile, expansile mass**; rupture causes sudden back or abdominal pain, shock and a high mortality. Ultrasound screening is offered to older male smokers in many countries.

**Coarctation** (narrowing near the ligamentum arteriosum) causes upper-limb hypertension, weak, delayed femoral pulses (**radiofemoral delay**) and **rib notching** on X-ray from enlarged intercostal collaterals; it is associated with bicuspid aortic valve and **intracranial aneurysms**.

Spinal cord ischemia after thoracoabdominal aortic surgery is a feared complication because the **artery of Adamkiewicz** (usually T9–T12, left side) may be sacrificed; **lumbar CSF drainage** is used to protect the cord, a direct overlap with neurosurgical practice.

Treatment in general terms: strict blood pressure and heart rate control, open surgical repair with grafts, and **endovascular stent-grafts (EVAR/TEVAR)**.

keyPoints: Largest artery; leaves the left ventricle via the aortic valve
Parts: ascending, arch, descending thoracic, abdominal
Arch branches: brachiocephalic, left common carotid, left subclavian
Passes the diaphragm at T12; splits into common iliacs at L4
Dissection: tearing pain to the back; Type A = surgical emergency

test.q: Which is NOT a direct branch of the aortic arch?
test.explain: The right common carotid comes from the brachiocephalic trunk, not directly from the arch.

test.q: At about which vertebral level does the aorta split into the common iliac arteries?
test.explain: The aortic bifurcation sits around L4, near the level of the umbilicus.

test.q: A Stanford Type A aortic dissection involves the:
test.explain: Type A involves the ascending aorta and usually needs emergency surgery.

test.q: Which nerve hooks under the aortic arch and can be compressed by an arch aneurysm, causing hoarseness?
test.explain: The left recurrent laryngeal loops under the arch beside the ligamentum arteriosum.

test.q: The artery the surgeon worries about for spinal cord supply during thoracoabdominal aortic repair is the artery of ______.
test.explain: It feeds the anterior spinal artery in the lower cord; losing it can cause paraplegia.
